meta.notes: Most sources on agent disputes are chargeback/PSP vendors with a commercial interest; survey figures (PYMNTS, Ravelin, Darwinium) are quoted as reported by secondary pages. No primary network rulebook text was fetchable. No public data exists on agent-dispute frequency or cost. Founder-listed Justt, Midigator, Skyfire and Nekuda pages were unfetchable (403/robots) and are not included as competitors; Payman's site shows it now targets banks. Prospects: only 9 primary-ICP companies were found with fetchable evidence (target was 20+); most DTC sites lack a fetchable about page with location or headcount, so size is omitted for all and location verified for 2. No contacts were added (none named with title on the companies' own fetchable pages).

evidence.title: When the First Agent Purchase Gets Disputed
evidence.quote: Today's chargeback process asks a binary question: did the cardholder authorize this transaction? Agentic commerce produces a harder case. The account was valid. The spending limit held. The merchant processed correctly.
evidence.statement: Industry newsletter describes a new dispute type: a valid, in-limit agent purchase the user did not intend, which the binary authorization test does not handle.

evidence.title: When the First Agent Purchase Gets Disputed
evidence.quote: No agent-specific reason code (Visa or Mastercard) … No mandate-content field in dispute files … No decision-trace representment standard
evidence.statement: Public Visa/Mastercard dispute guides have no agent reason code, no mandate field and no decision-trace representment standard.

evidence.title: Agentic Payments and Chargebacks: A Merchant Guide
evidence.quote: A disputed agent purchase files under a reason code you already work with, most often Visa 10.4, 13.1, or 13.3. Nothing in the dispute system labels a transaction as agent-made.
evidence.statement: Agent disputes are filed under existing reason codes and are not labelled as agent-made, so merchants cannot distinguish them in dispute data.

evidence.title: Agentic Payments and Chargebacks: A Merchant Guide
evidence.quote: Today's tools can't capture the mandate that proves an agent stayed inside the customer's limits. That mandate is what an agent dispute comes down to.
evidence.statement: A chargeback-alert vendor says current tools cannot capture the mandate, which is what agent disputes turn on.

evidence.title: AI Agent Chargeback Liability: Who Pays & How to Prepare
evidence.quote: A disputed agent purchase follows ordinary card-not-present rules, so the merchant pays unless it wins representment or the agent used a tokenized, authenticated network flow that shifts fraud liability to the issuer.
evidence.statement: Under current rules the merchant bears the loss on a disputed agent purchase unless it wins representment or a tokenized network flow shifts fraud liability.

evidence.title: Agentic commerce liability is still being written | Insights | Worldpay
evidence.quote: When an agent authenticates properly and a token is issued correctly, liability generally follows existing authenticated tokenized-transaction rules, with the issuer carrying fraud risk and the cardholder's chargeback rights intact.
evidence.statement: For fraud claims on properly authenticated, tokenized agent payments the issuer, not the merchant, generally carries the risk, which narrows merchant exposure.

evidence.title: Agentic commerce liability is still being written | Insights | Worldpay
evidence.quote: A shopper who claims their agent misunderstood an instruction, bought the wrong item or acted outside what they authorized is making a dispute claim, not a fraud claim. Today's frameworks don't yet have a clean answer for who absorbs that.
evidence.statement: Worldpay says non-fraud agent disputes (misunderstood instruction, out-of-scope purchase) have no clear liability answer.

evidence.title: Agentic commerce liability is still being written | Insights | Worldpay
evidence.quote: Without a signed mandate proving what the shopper authorized, a disagreement between agent and shopper becomes a coin flip, and issuers tend to side with the cardholder.

summary.statement: Merchants currently cannot distinguish agent disputes in dispute data: they are filed under existing reason codes (mainly Visa 10.4, 13.1, 13.3) and nothing labels them as agent-made.
Public Visa and Mastercard dispute guides have no agent-specific reason code and no mandate-content field.
Non-fraud agent disputes (agent misunderstood an instruction or acted outside scope) are dispute claims with no clean liability answer today.
Acquirers such as Worldpay are starting to detect agent transactions at the gateway, which could give merchants an agent flag upstream of the dispute.
By default the merchant bears the loss on a disputed agent purchase, as merchant of record, unless it wins representment or a tokenized network flow shifts fraud liability to the issuer.
For properly authenticated, tokenized agent payments, fraud-claim risk generally sits with the issuer, which narrows merchant exposure to non-fraud disputes.
General chargeback labour costs are visible: one merchant paid a freelancer $40 per case, another saved 199 hours by automating.
No public data quantifies revenue or labour lost to agent-initiated disputes specifically; the monthly cost per merchant remains unknown.
In the mid-market merchants found, chargebacks were owned by customer-experience or customer-support managers (or an outsourced freelancer), not a Head of Fraud.
The existing paid budget line is chargeback automation sold on contingency (Chargeflow: 25% of recovered amounts).
On the issuer/processor side, dedicated dispute managers run dispute data, BPO vendors and tooling.
The hypothesis' buyer (Head of Fraud/VP Payments) may be wrong for mid-market merchants; CX/operations may hold this budget.
Dispute experts and PSPs point to the signed mandate as the deciding evidence: without it, issuers tend to side with the cardholder.
Checkout.com lists the elements to capture: agent identifiers and signatures, mandate creation and approval events, and execution signals such as session tokens and orchestration traces.
Networks have not published agent-specific evidence requirements: no mandate field, no decision-trace representment standard.
AP2 defines no mandate retention or archive, and most consent records still do not reach merchants automatically.
A signed mandate proves what was bought, not that it matched what the user meant, so mandate evidence may not decide 'wrong item within mandate' disputes.
Merchants handle agent disputes with their existing chargeback stack: alert networks (Ethoca, Verifi) and automation vendors such as Chargeflow.

Incumbents are building the mandate-evidence layer themselves: Mastercard Verifiable Intent, Google AP2, PayPal's AP2-based dispute workflow, Stripe scoped tokens, Chargebacks911 UDMS consent trails and Worldpay agent detection.
American Express sidesteps the problem on its network by covering erroneous registered-agent purchases.
Agent purchase volume is still small: UK/US merchants report about 3% of transactions involve AI agents, and almost no shoppers plan to buy through agents yet.
ChatGPT Instant Checkout was retired in March 2026 after fewer than about 30 Shopify merchants turned it on, and in most implementations the user still confirms the final purchase.
There is no public data on how often agent purchases are disputed, and such disputes are not labelled in dispute systems.

hypothesis_update.problem: Merchants accepting AI-agent-initiated orders may face non-fraud disputes ('my agent bought the wrong thing') that land under ordinary reason codes, with no standard mandate record reaching the merchant; volume is very small today.
hypothesis_update.users: Customer-experience/support and payments-operations staff who handle chargebacks at e-commerce merchants; dispute operations at PSPs.
hypothesis_update.buyer: At mid-market merchants, often the CX/operations lead who owns chargeback tooling; at PSPs and acquirers, dispute/risk product owners.
hypothesis_update.decision_maker: Head of operations/finance at mid-market merchants; head of disputes or risk product at PSPs and acquirers.
hypothesis_update.economic_value: Win non-fraud agent disputes and cut manual chargeback labour (merchants already pay per case or a 25% contingency on recoveries); unquantified for agent disputes today.

rationale.statement: Agent disputes are filed under existing codes and are not labelled as agent-made.
At the mid-market merchants found, chargebacks were owned by CX/support managers or freelancers.
Agent transaction volume is small today (about 3% of transactions per merchants surveyed).

new_unknowns.question: Will card networks (Mastercard Verifiable Intent, AP2 via FIDO) deliver mandate records to merchants and PSPs directly, leaving no room for a neutral cross-protocol record?
What share of agent-initiated disputes are 'wrong item within mandate' cases that a mandate record cannot win?
